title: Hallmarks of AI writing: A guide for founders who write
gist: a16z crypto's editorial lead argues AI-detection discourse is the wrong frame: the 'tells' of machine prose (empty insight-shaped phrases, fungible low-friction diction, default over-structuring, em dashes) are pre-existing writing failures, and the only durable test is whether the writing does its job. The practical payload for founders is a taxonomy of when to edit versus embrace each habit, plus prompts that use LLMs for detection and structure rather than for voice. Note: the on-page headline reads 'Habits of AI writing, and what to do about them,' differing from the record title.

insights.claim: The two default assumptions of AI-writing discourse — that machine prose has identifiable tells and that any text containing them is bad — are both wrong, because humans have always produced the same patterns without AI.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Detector-percentage screening of founder or portfolio comms is a false signal; evaluate output on clarity and trustworthiness instead of provenance.
insights.quote: Arguments about AI writing tend to rely on two assumptions: (1) that machine-generated prose can be identified by a conspicuous set of tells, and (2) that anything containing those tells is necessarily bad and embarrassing. Respectfully, these are terrible ways to think about writing.

insights.claim: The durable evaluation rubric for any text — human, model, or hybrid — is four questions: does it explain clearly, can readers trust it, is a decision-maker behind the wheel, and is it doing its job.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A provenance-agnostic quality bar that survives every future model release; usable directly as an editorial standard for comms and research output.
insights.quote: Does it explain things clearly? Can readers trust it? Is someone — anyone — behind the wheel, making decisions here? In short, is the writing doing its job?
insights.locator: We writers can pontificate about what AI

insights.claim: In crypto specifically, the twin noise sources are AI-written scams and human-written jargon, both of which obscure a project's actual goals and values.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Diligence heuristic: opaque jargon in a crypto project's own writing is as much a red flag as obviously synthetic promotional copy.
insights.quote: scams (often written by AI) and jargon (too often written by humans) can easily distract from real goals and values.
insights.locator: They're also useful in industries like ours

insights.claim: Asking whether a given piece is machine-generated is becoming pointless because the honest answer will almost always be 'to some degree,' leaving only narrow cases — required disclosure, byline-is-the-point authorship, and one person impersonating a thousand — where detection genuinely matters.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Narrows the real market for AI-detection and proof-of-personhood tooling to disclosure compliance and sybil/impersonation defense rather than general-purpose content screening.
insights.quote: the egregious cases of AI writing still need outing, whether by our own standards or Proof of Person technologies: for example, when disclosure is required, when the human on the byline is the whole point, or when one person is pretending to be a thousand.
insights.locator: As more people use these tools, interrogating

insights.claim: Abandoning a punctuation mark invented at the dawn of printing purely to avoid resembling a machine is an absurd concession that shows people are deferring to LLMs rather than using them.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Signals the cultural cycle where AI aesthetics reshape human behavior faster than the underlying quality bar — a pattern worth watching in any medium models colonize.
insights.quote: why are we showing LLMs this kind of deference at all? We would relinquish an entire punctuation mark — an innovation conceived at the dawn of printing! — all to avoid looking like a machine helped us.
insights.locator: Finally, with all of the hand-wringing over

insights.claim: The hardest AI tell to spot is not lists or em dashes but sentences that look and sound like sentences while meaning nothing — 'Something real is happening,' 'The implications are significant' — which models generate in bulk as plausible connective tissue.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: This is the category that survives every surface-level edit pass, so it is where an editor's or reader's attention pays the highest return.
insights.quote: these sentences don't actually look like a problem. They just kind of look like sentences.
insights.locator: Rhetorical hallmarks: Insight-shaped writing

insights.claim: The operational test for empty profundity is the paraphrase test: restate the sentence, keep the better version, and delete it entirely if it reduces to 'stuff exists' or 'things are changing.'
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A single reusable edit rule that removes the highest-cost class of filler; can be run as an LLM prompt by asking for the 'boring' version.
insights.quote: They're phrases that sound weighty but generally lack the specificity to survive paraphrase.
insights.locator: AI writing produces these sorts of phrases

insights.claim: So-called AI filler is really the older category of corporate business-blog speak — 'We're excited to announce,' 'We're at an inflection point,' 'the next chapter of our journey' — and it is first-draft language rather than lazy writing.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Reframes model output as a legitimate starting point rather than a disqualifier, which is the permissive stance a fund takes toward founders using these tools.
insights.quote: Before it became associated with AI writing, we used to call this category of bland, meaningless language corporate, because it's your typical, dispassionate business-blog speak.
insights.locator: AI writing produces these sorts of phrases

insights.claim: Five named rhetorical tells should be edited almost always and embraced almost never: naturally essenced profundity, empty contrasts ('it's not just about X — it's about Y' where Y is fuzzier), hedges, excessive parallelism, and in-summation phrases.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist usable as a prompt or style-guide seed for any founder or team publishing at volume.
insights.quote: Meaningless, gobbledygook language is at the top of our stack-ranked list of writing pitfalls. It will never move your ideas forward, no matter how nice it sounds. It is a scourge.
insights.locator: Some tells and when to edit them

insights.claim: Hedges are the one rhetorical tell with a legitimate exemption: in finance and healthcare, hedging language is 'load-bearing' because it softens claims for legal compliance.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Regulated-industry comms cannot be de-hedged by a blanket LLM pass without creating legal exposure — a real constraint on automated editing tools in those verticals.
insights.quote: Note that in some industries, like finance or healthcare, some hedges are necessary to soften claims and comply with the law. I think AI would call these "load-bearing" hedges.
insights.locator: Hedges. "In many ways."

insights.claim: Default AI prose draws on roughly four hundred of the English language's million words, so the useful test is fungibility — whether a sentence could be lifted verbatim into a stranger's essay on a different topic unnoticed.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: The 'transplant test' is a faster, more durable filter than any banned-word list, which model updates immediately obsolete.
insights.quote: There are roughly one million words in the English language. Default AI writing sounds like it's working with about four hundred of them.
insights.locator: Voice hallmarks: Alexa voice

insights.claim: Distinctive prose is a business asset for founders because people increasingly market on the strength of their personalities, with Brian Armstrong (pithy, earnest, unironic), Vitalik Buterin (technical, digressive, dense), and Chris Dixon (austere, philosophical) as recognizable voice signatures.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Founder voice is distribution: ceding it to an LLM erases a differentiator that compounds in attention-driven markets like crypto.
insights.quote: It's why we can so easily conjure what it means to write like Brian Armstrong (pithy, earnest, unironic); like Vitalik Buterin (technical, digressive, dense); or like Chris Dixon (austere, philosophical).
insights.locator: In the meantime, thoughtful diction isn't just

insights.claim: Banned-word lists are a losing game because the vocabulary tells rotate — 'delve' spiked in academic abstracts after ChatGPT's 2022 launch, then tapestry, testament and underscore, then load-bearing, scaffolding and broader.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Any product or policy built on static lexical AI-tells decays within a model generation; only structural tests like fungibility persist.
insights.quote: Researchers famously noticed the word "delve" spiking in academic abstracts after ChatGPT launched in 2022, and an onslaught of banned-word lists followed
insights.locator: For a while you could track this

insights.claim: Generic 'Alexa voice' is the correct choice at scale — support docs, error messages, terms of service, safety instructions and mass apologies — because personality becomes friction when a million strangers read the same text in a million contexts.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Defines exactly where fully automated, voiceless model output is not just acceptable but preferable — the near-term commodity layer of AI writing.
insights.quote: Here, personality is friction and Alexa voice is a mercy.
insights.locator: Embrace: When being an NPC is kind

insights.claim: Vagueness is fixed by naming the mechanism: 'The Ethereum ecosystem is expanding' becomes 'Developers are building more wallets, exchanges, and lending markets around Ethereum.'
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A transferable specificity drill for research and pitch writing — replace abstractions like ecosystem, landscape and space with the concrete things being built.
insights.quote: "The Ethereum ecosystem is expanding" can become, with a little more specificity, "Developers are building more wallets, exchanges, and lending markets around Ethereum."
insights.locator: Go through your laundry list of vague

themes.theme: Structure is a decision, not a default

insights.claim: Structure should be treated as an explicit set of decisions — which container, which information leads, which ideas group, and what to call them — with the right answer determined by the job to be done, not by a template.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Explains why model defaults fail: they optimize structure independent of function, so the human contribution is format selection, not prose.
insights.quote: Structure is a set of decisions — which container to use, which information matters most, which ideas go together, and what to call them. The right decisions depend on the job to be done.
insights.locator: Structural hallmarks: All form, no function

insights.claim: Different genres impose different structural requirements: a narrative essay needs discovery and tension, a product announcement needs brutal efficiency to catch mid-scroll readers, and an explainer needs sequentially building concepts.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Concrete mapping from content goal to format, and the reason a single house style applied across all company comms underperforms.
insights.quote: A narrative essay needs discovery and tension to keep readers moving. A product announcement needs to be brutally efficient to catch readers mid-scroll.
insights.locator: A good, clear structure helps readers immediately

insights.claim: Heavy structure — headers, bullets, taxonomies — should be embraced rather than edited out when optimizing for LLMs and search engines, which reward well-structured information, and for reference content people navigate rather than read once.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Direct tension between anti-AI-slop aesthetics and machine discoverability: content built for LLM retrieval should look more like AI writing, not less.
insights.quote: When optimizing for LLMs and search engines, which reward well-structured information.
insights.locator: Embrace: When the structure of a piece

insights.claim: Imposing list structure on a story materially changes its meaning, since a numbered list of reasons a startup pivoted reads differently from the narrative of how the pivot happened even when the facts are identical.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A caution for anyone summarizing company narratives into bullets — the reformatting silently alters the claim being made.
insights.quote: a numbered list of reasons a startup pivoted reads very differently than the story of how it happened, even when facts are the same
insights.locator: When structure dilutes or changes your meaning

insights.claim: As writers avoid em dashes to escape AI suspicion, models are already routing around them with colons, meaning any punctuation-based tell will be arbitraged away and the current meta must change by definition.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Signal degradation is structural: every published detection heuristic trains its own evasion, which caps the long-run value of stylometric AI detection.
insights.quote: Now that people are bending over backward to avoid em dashes, AI itself is routing around them with colons. Shall we start using interrobangs to look appropriately human?!
insights.locator: Punctuation hallmarks: The em dash panic

insights.claim: The real punctuation tell is sameness and density rather than any individual mark — consecutive colon-led lists and repeated em dash asides exhaust readers, with a practical ceiling of two em dashes per sentence.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Gives an actionable, mark-agnostic edit rule that survives the meta churn: check distribution, not presence.
insights.quote: There's not really a numerical limit on the number of em dashes you can use in a sentence, but don't use more than two.
insights.locator: Em dash clustering. Not the dash itself

insights.claim: Reading writing aloud and treating punctuation as stage directions is the recommended test, on the theory that anything sounding unnatural aloud will register as wrong to readers too.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A zero-tooling QA check that catches the sameness problem no detector currently scores.
insights.quote: A good test is reading your writing aloud, using punctuation like stage directions.
insights.locator: Another punctuation-related hallmark to look out for

themes.theme: How to actually use the models

insights.claim: LLMs are better deployed as detectors than as writers, because models are very good at identifying jargon, business-speak, and hedging in a draft even when their own generated prose is full of it.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: The defensible product wedge is critique and diagnosis in the editing loop, not first-draft generation — a different workflow position than most AI writing tools occupy.
insights.quote: Many of these tips focus on using LLMs for detection, not for writing. Models are actually very good at identifying jargon, business-speak, and other words frequently used in AI writing.
insights.locator: Tips: Many of these tips focus on

insights.claim: Instructing a model to 'remove all em dashes' fails because it substitutes other marks while preserving the same underlying sentence structure; the working prompt is to default to periods and commas and use special punctuation only when grammatically required.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that surface-level style prompts do not change model syntax — instructions must target structure to have effect.
insights.quote: Avoid the urge to tell a model to "remove all em dashes." It will often just replace them with something else, while preserving the same underlying sentence structure.
insights.locator: Tips: Don't overthink whether punctuation is making

insights.claim: A personal style guide with examples and counterexamples, plus feeding the model samples of writing you admire to build a 'punctuation fingerprint,' outlasts any laundry list of AI tells.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Points to persistent per-user style artifacts as the durable layer of AI writing tooling, versus disposable tell-lists.
insights.quote: This will hold up better than a laundry list of AI tells.
insights.locator: Creating a rough style guide that defines

insights.claim: Reverse-outlining a published piece in the target genre — prompting the LLM to describe the function each paragraph serves — produces a reusable skeleton for drafting, and the structural thinking pays off even when the model's output is poor.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: A repeatable prompt pattern for producing genre-correct structure rather than default model structure.
insights.quote: Paste a published piece in the same genre, and prompt it to create a "reverse-outline," describing the function each paragraph serves.

insights.claim: Feeding voice notes into an LLM is an emerging drafting workflow whose underappreciated benefit is surfacing personal idiosyncrasies that differentiate a writer's voice, though the output always requires editing.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: Voice-to-draft is a growing usage pattern with a differentiation angle beyond mere speed — relevant to anyone building in the dictation-to-writing stack.
insights.quote: people are starting to feed voice notes into LLMs as a way to get words on paper. An underappreciated benefit is finding personal idiosyncrasies that set your voice apart.
insights.locator: Finally, people are starting to feed voice

insights.claim: AI's net effect on writing is expansionary rather than degrading: it gets ideas published that would otherwise never be written down, saves time on organization and research, and may make people better writers.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Zinn
insights.so_what: The house view from a major crypto/tech investor's editorial function — volume of published ideas rises, so attention and curation, not production, become the scarce goods.
insights.quote: AI helps people articulate and publish ideas they'd otherwise never write down. It can save time on organization and research. It may even help us become better writers.
insights.locator: AI helps people articulate and publish ideas
